title: Why have a court hierarchy

match.reason: The new point explains why the court hierarchy exists, while the closest bank point, Appeals, covers how an appeal works and what each side can challenge, so it is related rather than the same idea and the other two points are unrelated.

draft.title: Why have a court hierarchy
card: A court hierarchy ranks courts from the lowest to the highest. In Victoria the criminal courts run from the Magistrates' Court, to the County Court, to the Supreme Court, then the Court of Appeal.

Each court hears cases of a set seriousness and type. Less serious cases go to lower courts, and the most serious go to higher courts. Courts can then build skill and use resources to suit the cases they hear.
A party who thinks a court made a mistake may ask a higher court to review the decision. The hierarchy gives them somewhere to go.
Appeals can also correct errors in law and help the law stay consistent, as lower courts follow the decisions of higher courts.
draft.remember: A hierarchy sorts cases by seriousness and gives a path to appeal.

a.q: Which is a reason for having a court hierarchy?
opts: It lets a party ask a higher court to review a decision
It lets every case be heard in the highest court
It means each court hears only one kind of crime
It lets the lowest court overrule the higher courts
a.why: A hierarchy gives a path for appeal to a higher court. It does not put every case in the highest court, because cases are sorted by seriousness. Courts are not limited to a single crime, and lower courts do not overrule higher ones.
a.clue: Think about where a party goes if they think a court got it wrong.

b.q: Dev is charged with a minor traffic offence, and Priya is charged with a very serious offence. Why does the hierarchy help with their cases?
opts: Each case can go to a court suited to its seriousness
Both cases can be heard by the same magistrate
Each case must be appealed before it is heard
Priya's case can skip the hearing and go to appeal
b.why: The hierarchy sends less serious cases to lower courts and more serious cases to higher courts. This is specialisation by seriousness. Appeals come after a decision, so a case is not appealed before it is heard.
b.clue: The two charges differ in how serious they are.

a.best: It lets a party ask a higher court to review a decision

b.best: Each case can go to a court suited to its seriousness

problems.detail: The card lists 'the Supreme Court, then the Court of Appeal' as if they were separate courts. The Court of Appeal is a division of the Supreme Court of Victoria. The hierarchy should read Magistrates' Court, County Court, Supreme Court (Trial Division), Supreme Court (Court of Appeal). The card could also mention that the High Court of Australia sits above these courts.
